findings.paper_title: 02. Treasury management year end report 2025-26
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates ranged from 4.59% to 5.48% over the year; average 4.84%
findings.detail: Long-term borrowing rates offered by the PWLB showed significant volatility during 2025/26, with 10-year rates ranging from a low of 4.59% to a high of 5.48%. The average rate for the period was 4.84%. The report notes that the financial year was dominated by two periods of significant uncertainty: US trade tariffs in April 2025 and the US/Israel war with Iran in February 2026, both of which drove market volatility.
findings.matters: The council executed most of its refinancing and new borrowing during a volatile rate environment. The average rate of 4.84% is materially higher than rates available in prior years. Any delay in refinancing existing debt exposes the council to the risk of locking in these elevated rates. The geopolitical and trade uncertainty noted is ongoing.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB rates: low 4.59%, high 5.48%, average 4.84%
findings.quote: As shown in the graph in section 5.11, the rates for long term borrowing continue to be volatile, with the lowest rate on a PWLB 10-year EIP loan in the period being 4.59% and the highest being 5.48%. The average rate for the period was 4.84%.

findings.paper_title: 02. Treasury management year end report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pooled fund investments carry £1.4m unrealised loss; market value £27.6m on £29m originally invested
findings.detail: The council holds £29m in strategic pooled funds (property, bond, equity, multi-asset) with a current market value of £27.6m, representing an unrealised loss of £1.4m. This loss is absorbed by a separate unusable reserve under a statutory override that continues until 1 April 2029 for legacy investments. The council notes that as a net borrower, the holding of these long-term investments will be kept under review, and a decision may be taken to exit when viable.
findings.matters: The council is holding investments at a loss while carrying net borrowing of £649.4m. There is an implicit signal that the council may liquidate these funds if market conditions allow, which could affect cash flow projections. The statutory override provides breathing room until 2029, but the override ends on 1 April 2028 for non-legacy investments.
findings.figures: £29m invested; £27.6m market value; £1.4m unrealised loss; statutory override continues until 1 April 2029
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the County Council held £29.0m in a number of diversified pooled funds. The market value of these investments was £27.6m, representing a capital loss of £1.4m on the amount originally invested. However, given that the County Council is a net borrower, the holding of these long-term investments will be kept under review and a decision may be taken to exit from these funds when viable to do so.

findings.paper_title: 02. Treasury management year end report 2025-26
findings.headline: New long-term borrowing of £215m undertaken in year; includes £130.6m for capital programme and £84.4m for debt refinancing
findings.detail: The council undertook significant new borrowing of £215m during 2025/26. This comprised £130.6m to fund the capital programme and £84.4m to refinance external debt (including the LOBO repayment and commercial debt prepayment noted above). The council's stated strategy is gradual borrowing to avoid having to borrow significantly when rates spike.
findings.matters: Total borrowing of £215m is material and shows the council's sustained capital financing need. The split between funding new investment (£130.6m) and refinancing (£84.4m) is important for understanding whether the council is growing its debt stock or managing the maturity profile. The gradual approach is prudent, but rates have been volatile.
findings.figures: £215m new long-term borrowing; £130.6m for capital programme; £84.4m for debt refinancing
findings.quote: During the year to 31 March 2026, new long-term borrowing of £215m was undertaken, this included £130.6m to fund the capital programme plus £84.4m to refinance external debt (as set out in sections 8.10 and 8.13).

findings.paper_title: 02. Treasury management year end report 2025-26
findings.headline: LOBO loan of £9.4m called for refinancing; council repaid and refinanced through PWLB
findings.detail: In June 2025, the council was notified of an intended rate increase on a LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loan. The council exercised its option to repay the £9.4m loan at no additional cost and refinanced it through the PWLB. LOBO loans carry inherent refinancing risk because the lender can force a rate increase at set dates.
findings.matters: This shows active management of refinancing risk but also demonstrates that the council was exposed to forced refinancing at an inopportune time. The council removed £9.4m of LOBO exposure, which is favourable, but signals that commercial lenders were tightening terms.
findings.figures: £9.4m LOBO loan repaid; refinanced through PWLB
findings.quote: At the start of the financial year, the Authority held £19.4m of LOBO's (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where the lender has the option to propose an increase in the interest rate at set dates, following which the County Council has the option to either accept the new rate or to repay the loan at no additional cost. In June 2025, the County Council was notified of an intended increase in the rate on one of its outstanding LOBO loans and consequently took the decision to repay the £9.4m loan and has subsequently refinanced this through a loan from the PWLB.

findings.paper_title: 02. Treasury management year end report 2025-26
findings.headline: £91m commercial debt prepaid at discount; new PWLB loans at higher rates (5.35%) but offset by reduced principal; annual revenue benefit £1.6m
findings.detail: In July 2025, the council prepaid £91m of commercial bank loans carrying an average rate of 4.46%, achieving a redemption cost of £75m. This negotiated discount of £16m (17.6% reduction) will be amortised over 10 years, yielding annual revenue benefit of £1.6m. The redeemed loans were refinanced with PWLB medium-term loans at higher rates (5.35%), but the council benefits from paying interest on a reduced principal amount.
findings.matters: The council took advantage of a window to lock in debt savings. However, it has shifted to higher nominal rates (5.35% vs 4.46%), creating exposure if rates fall further. The £1.6m annual benefit helps offset future budget pressures but represents a timing-dependent strategic choice.
findings.figures: £91m commercial loans repaid; redemption cost £75m; discount £16m; replacement rate 5.35%; annual benefit £1.6m amortised over 10 years
findings.quote: In July 2025, the County Council prepaid £91m of loans from commercial banks running at an average rate of 4.46%, at a redemption cost of £75m. In line with capital finance regulations, the discount of £16m (the difference between the loan principal and redemption cost) will be amortised over 10 years, providing an annual revenue benefit of £1.6m for the Council. The redeemed loans have been refinanced by medium-term loans from the PWLB. While the new loans are at higher interest rates (5.35%), this will be offset by savings generated by paying interest on a reduced loan principal.

findings.paper_title: 02. Treasury management year end report 2025-26
findings.headline: £83m High Needs deficit is a significant contributor to underlying borrowing requirement; funding contingent on DfE approval expected September 2026
findings.detail: The council holds a £83m deficit in the High Needs block (dedicated schools grant for SEND). This deficit drives borrowing and interest costs. The council is awaiting government funding to cover 90% of the deficit via the High Needs Stability Grant, contingent on DfE approval of the Local Area SEND Reform Plan. Notification expected September 2026, with funding release in Autumn; if amendments are required, funding slips to February 2027. After the accounting override ends 1 April 2028, SEND spending moves to government departmental budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that nearly £83m of the council's borrowing requirement is driven by education funding pressures outside its control, and that relief depends on DfE approval in a specific window. Slippage to February 2027 would delay relief by six months.
findings.figures: £83m deficit; 90% to be funded; funding release September 2026 or February 2027 if amendments required; override ends 1 April 2028
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the £83m High Needs deficit represents a significant contributor to the Council's underlying borrowing requirement and associated interest costs. The settlement announced the funding of 90% of the deficit as at 31st March 2026 via the new High Needs Stability Grant. Payment of this grant is contingent on agreement of the recently submitted Local Area SEND Reform Plan by the Department for Education. Should the plan be agreed, notification is expected in September 2026 with funding released in the Autumn. Should amendments be required, subject to further review and approval, funding would be received in February 2027.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital receipts fell £3m short of the £26.9m budgeted, with recovery delayed into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council assumed £26.9m of capital receipts but achieved only £21.7m. The shortfall is attributed to a property sale delayed by conveyancing, expected to complete in early 2026/27. However, this ties the 2026/27 capital programme to timely completion of asset disposals.
findings.matters: The capital programme's financing plan depends on timely asset sales. A delay of even a few weeks from early 2026/27 into the new financial year creates in-year funding pressure; further slippage would require borrowing or programme cuts.
findings.figures: £26.9m assumed; £21.7m achieved; £3.0m shortfall
findings.quote: Capital receipts totalling £21.7m were achieved by 31st March 2026 representing a shortfall of (£3.0m).

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Older People services income down £3.5m, driven by fewer full-cost payers than demographic trends predict
findings.detail: The council budgeted for full-cost payer income to grow in line with demographic trends (rising older population), but instead saw a significant reduction in the number of full-cost payers. This cost the service £3.5m and the council flags it as an ongoing and principal risk into 2026/27. The Income Transformation programme is reviewing drivers.
findings.matters: The council's income assumptions for social care are proving optimistic; either demographics are different than modeled, or take-up of chargeable care is lower. This is material to 2026/27 forecasting and may indicate the council is underestimating need for council-funded care.
findings.figures: £3.5m shortfall against budgeted Older People income
findings.quote: Income received is £3.5m below budget, driven primarily by a significant reduction in the number of full‑cost payers, which would normally be expected to increase in line with demographic growth. This reduction represents the principal and ongoing risk into 2026/27, as it has a sustained impact on income levels.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Year-end position dependent on one-off financial measures that cannot be sustained
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the headline balanced position was supported by temporary measures including capitalisation of expenditure, grant re-direction, and release of provisions. These actions do not address underlying cost and demand pressures, and the council notes they cannot be relied upon in future years. The council is aware this represents a structural imbalance being masked.
findings.matters: The council's own assessment is that the 2025/26 position overstates underlying financial health. If one-off measures are not available in 2026/27, the baseline overspend could be significantly larger than reported.
findings.figures: £0.8m reported overspend masked by one-off measures; £10m contingency used
findings.quote: However, while the headline position is positive, it is important to recognise that it has been supported in part by a range of temporary, one-off financial measures. These include the use of corporate actions such as grant adjustments, capital accounting flexibilities and the release of provisions, which have helped to offset in-year pressures. While these measures have been used appropriately, they do not fully address the underlying drivers of cost and demand and cannot be relied upon in future years.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme £44.3m reprogrammed into future years; major schemes consistently delayed
findings.detail: Expenditure came in £20.0m below budget, but £44.3m was reprogrammed into future years. Delays span highways (procurement and weather), school infrastructure (planning and contractor capacity), Harlow Gilston (legal challenges), SEND place planning (biodiversity net gain and contract delays), bus improvements, and Zero Emission Bus scheme (global supply chain issues and legal agreements). The council acknowledges this highlights risks around delivery capacity.
findings.matters: A reprogramming of this scale (15% of the £294.5m budget) into future years, with delays driven by factors outside the council's control (planning, contractor capacity, supply chain), suggests the council's project delivery governance may be weak or optimistic assumptions are built into future planning.
findings.figures: £44.3m reprogrammed; £20.0m underspend; total revised budget £294.5m
findings.quote: The capital programme has experienced actual expenditure lower than budgeted for, with a £20.0m underspend and £44.3m of expenditure reprogrammed into future years. This reflects delays across a range of major schemes, including highways, school infrastructure and place-based developments, driven by factors such as procurement challenges, planning processes, contractor capacity and wider market conditions.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Savings programme £1.6m short of target, with non-delivery concentrated in property, waste, and income
findings.detail: Of the £42.0m savings target, only £40.4m was achieved (96.2%), a shortfall of £1.6m. The council cites policy delays on waste management savings, the failure of the Apsley site property sale after the seller withdrew, and unmet income generation targets in libraries. The council also notes that replicating non-pay savings from 2024/25 is proving more challenging, suggesting one-off gains may not recur.
findings.matters: This mix of structural failures (property sale falling through, policy delays in waste) and income shortfalls indicates the council is relying on savings that are not reliably repeatable. If the 2026/27 programme has similar targets, delivery risk is elevated.
findings.figures: £40.4m achieved of £42.0m target; £1.6m shortfall (3.8%)
findings.quote: delivery of £40.4m of the £42.0m savings programme, with the £1.6m of savings not achieved primarily within Waste, property-related savings and income generating areas.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: £5.5m historical Direct Payments balances were unaccounted for, surfacing an internal controls weakness
findings.detail: A late-year review of Direct Payment balances identified £5.5m in historical account balances spanning several years. Of this, £2.8m relates to deceased individuals and will be written off; £2.6m may be recoverable but £1.1m provision was made for the risk it will not be collected. The issue meant £3.89m was included in the Adult Care overspend. The council has committed to strengthened processes and full procedure review.
findings.matters: This reveals a failure in reconciliation controls on a high-value, complex budget area. The scale and age of undetected balances suggests the monitoring was not rigorous, raising questions about control environment maturity.
findings.figures: £5.5m identified; £2.8m written off; £2.6m potentially recoverable; £1.1m provision; £3.89m impact on year-end outturn
findings.quote: a review of Direct Payment balances has identified an issue that has adversely affected the final outturn. The review aimed to recover unused Direct Payment funds, a standard practice across local authorities. While over £0.5m was successfully recovered between December 2025 and March 2026, further work identified historical balances totalling £5.5m across a large number of accounts, some dating back several years.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Children Looked After numbers accelerating faster than planned, with costs rising mid-year
findings.detail: CLA numbers grew from 828 in March 2024 to 935 by March 2026 (a 13% increase in just over a year), and the acceleration quickened: costs rose from £1.9m monthly in June 2025 to £2.2m by March 2026. The service overspent by £4.2m, and the council notes this will remain under ongoing review in 2026/27, suggesting the position is not yet stable.
findings.matters: A 13% annual growth rate in the highest-cost statutory service indicates demographic or safeguarding trends the council cannot control or predict. If this trajectory continues, it will breach the 2026/27 budget.
findings.figures: CLA numbers: 828 (March 2024) to 935 (March 2026); monthly costs £1.9m (June 2025) rising to £2.2m (March 2026); £4.2m overspend
findings.quote: Children Looked After (CLA) ended the year with an overspend of £4.2m, reflecting an increase in CLA numbers from 828 in March 2024 to 935 by March 2026. There has been a notable acceleration in costs during the year, rising from £1.9m in June 2025 to £2.2m by March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 260715 07 Q4 Finance Budget Monitor 2025-26
findings.headline: Schools High Needs Block has accumulated £83m deficit with no identified funding source
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block reached an £83.0m accumulated deficit by year-end, with a £9.9m in-year overspend. During 2025/26 alone, the cost of meeting local need exceeded government grant funding by more than £50 million. This is a structural funding gap that cannot be closed from the council's own resources.
findings.matters: This represents an unfunded statutory obligation that will constrain the council's financial flexibility for years; it must be disclosed to lenders as a contingent liability and signals demographic pressures the council cannot afford to meet.
findings.figures: £83.0m accumulated deficit; £9.9m in-year overspend; £50m+ annual funding gap
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block continues to face significant and growing deficits, with the cumulative deficit position reaching approximately £83m. During 2025/26, the cost of meeting local need exceeded available government grant funding by more than £50 million.

findings.paper_title: 05a. Appendix A HCC Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit opinion remains modified on prior-year comparatives, though expected to improve to fully unqualified for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's 2024/25 accounts received a modified audit opinion due to inability to audit comparatives from disclaimed 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts. This reflects prior control environment and audit resourcing issues in earlier years. However, the external auditor expects to issue an unqualified opinion for 2025/26, ahead of national timelines, indicating improvement in both control environment and audit progression.
findings.matters: Modified opinions, even when improving, indicate prior-period control or financial reporting issues; unqualified opinion expected for 2025/26 shows positive trend but does not eliminate earlier period concerns.
findings.figures: Council expected to reach unqualified 2025/26 opinion ahead of national timelines; most authorities anticipated to have qualified 2025/26 opinions

Slow implementation of audit recommendations suggests either resource constraints or weak governance of remediation activity, leaving identified control gaps open to risk.

findings.headline: Internal audit found control weaknesses in four significant service areas across children's and adult services
findings.detail: Four service audits received limited assurance opinions during 2025/26, indicating control weaknesses that may put at risk the achievement of objectives. The affected areas span critical services: Section 17 Payments and Care Leavers Service (children's services), SEND Accommodation and Homecare Commissioning (adult services), and Marketing/Advertising. Limited assurance across both service pillars suggests potential systemic issues beyond isolated failures.

findings.paper_title: 05a. Appendix A HCC Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: £2.2m in fraud and error remains under investigation in 34 cases, with £650k already confirmed from resolved investigations
findings.detail: Counter Fraud Service concluded 50 investigations in 2025/26, identifying £650k in confirmed fraud and error across 40 cases. The ongoing investigation may reveal additional losses and further control weaknesses.

findings.quote: Of 50 investigations concluded in year, 40 identified fraud or error totalling £650k with a further £2.2m in fraud and error (34 cases) still live and under investigation at year end.

findings.paper_title: 05a. Appendix A HCC Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Hertfordshire faces major governance uncertainty as Local Government Reorganisation proceeds towards creation of 2-4 new unitary councils by April 2028
findings.detail: The council submitted its LGR proposal to central government on 28 November 2025, outlining three options for two, three or four unitary councils. The Secretary of State's decision is expected summer 2026, followed by transition arrangements and governance structures for new authorities. This represents fundamental restructuring of the council's operating environment with accompanying risks to governance, financial control and service continuity during the transition period.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand major structural changes to the borrower's governance and operational model, including risks to financial control, service delivery and debt servicing during transition.

This outlined three different options of two, three or four unitary councils for the county.

While this is a specific service issue, it signals regulatory intervention into council-controlled delivery.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A - HCC 25-26 Draft Audit Plan
findings.headline: Triennial pension valuation at 31 March 2025 creates re-basing and potential for material changes to pension liabilities and contributions
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme triennial valuation at 31 March 2025 requires actuaries to re-base their models for actual experience since 2022, which could result in corrections to the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations. This also updates contributions payable, which could affect the asset ceiling applying to the council. Recent market conditions mean more councils are moving into pension surplus, with complex accounting requirements.
findings.matters: Pension deficits or surpluses affect the council's balance sheet and financial sustainability; a revaluation of actuarial assumptions could create material movements that a lender must understand.

This means re-basing their estimate models to allow for actual experience since 2022, which could result in corrections to the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations this year. It also updates the contributions payable, which could have an impact on the assessment of the asset ceiling applying to the Council.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A - HCC 25-26 Draft Audit Plan
findings.headline: Major asset revaluation policy change affecting £3,164m of land and buildings, with indexation assumption risk
findings.detail: The Code of Practice requires councils to move from rolling 3-year revaluation cycles to either quinquennial revaluation with annual indexation, or 5-year rolling revaluation with indexation in intervening years. Hertfordshire historically used 3-year rolling revaluation. The audit notes this creates risk that assets not revalued in year may differ materially from fair value due to inappropriate indexation applied.
findings.matters: A lender requires accurate asset valuations to assess the council's financial position; a major policy change affecting £3,164m of assets creates estimation uncertainty and the audit risk is explicitly elevated to significant.
findings.figures: £3,164m net book value of Land, Buildings & Surplus Assets in 24/25
findings.quote: The total net book value of Land, Buildings & Surplus Assets in 24/25 was £3,164m. This creates a risk that the carrying value of assets not revalued in year differs materially from the year end current value as the indexation applied is not appropriate.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A - HCC 25-26 Draft Audit Plan
findings.headline: Significant ongoing demand-driven cost pressures in statutory adult and children's social care services
findings.detail: Adult social care faces demand-led pressures driven by increases in the average cost of care packages and additional demand for high-cost nursing care. Children's services faces staffing pressures from increasing demand and agency costs for Educational Psychologists. Children Looked After placements overspent by £1.1m due to increased numbers and more complex cases. These are characterised as significant financial pressures.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-driven and mandatory; a lender must understand whether these cost pressures are structural and likely to persist or whether mitigation programmes are working.
findings.figures: Children's services overspend driven by £11.4m High Needs block; Children Looked After placements £1.1m overspent; Adult services facing demand-led pressures on nursing care costs
findings.quote: The main cause for the position was reported as significant financial pressures in relation to the delivery of statutory social care services. Adult services (Older People) faced demand led pressures driven by increases in the average cost of packages and additional demand for high-cost nursing care. In Children's Services, there were staffing pressures driven by increasing demand and the cost of agency to fill hard-to-recruit Educational Psychologists.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A - HCC 25-26 Draft Audit Plan
findings.headline: Savings target of £42m has a forecast adverse variance of £1.9m at Q3, with specific unmet milestones
findings.detail: The 2025-26 budget depends on delivering £42m of savings. At Q3, the council forecasts falling short by £1.9m. Specific shortfalls are: delays in Adult Care Services fees and charges due to IT issues, Growth and Environment new waste site booking systems on hold, and the Resources plan to purchase a property to reduce rent not yet achieved.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates the council's ability to balance its budget; a £1.9m shortfall on a £42m savings target (4.5% variance) signals delivery risk in key service areas.
findings.figures: £42m savings target; £1.9m adverse forecast variance; quarterly overspend forecast £1.4m (before £10m contingency)
findings.quote: At quarter three, the Council is forecasting an adverse variance of £1.9m against the savings plan. The majority of the variance can be attributed to forecasted underachievement in the following areas: delays in Adult Care Services achieving full savings on fees and charges target due to card provider software issues, Growth and Environment where new booking systems at waste sites have been put on hold, and in Resources the plan to purchase a site to reduce rent has not yet achieved.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A - HCC 25-26 Draft Audit Plan
findings.headline: High Needs funding block overspend of £11.6m for special educational needs and disabilities, described as ongoing pressure
findings.detail: The Schools budget carried an £11.4m overspend in 2025/26 Q3, driven almost entirely by the High Needs funding block which funds educational support for children with SEND and alternative provision. This is characterised as an ongoing pressure with mitigation plans in place. The government announced in February 2026 plans to cover 90% of local authority SEND deficits for 26/27.
findings.matters: SEND services are statutory and demand-driven; a lender will want to know whether the council can absorb or must finance this ongoing pressure, and whether government funding changes will materially improve the position.
findings.figures: £11.6m overspend in High Needs block; £11.4m total Schools overspend; government commitment to cover 90% of SEND deficits from 26/27
findings.quote: The overspend was driven by a £11.6m overspend being reported within the High Needs funding block, which is responsible for funding educational support for children with Special Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND) and those that require Alternative Provision. This has been an ongoing pressure through the year and there are savings plans in place to mitigate this increased spend.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A - HCC 25-26 Draft Audit Plan
findings.headline: Control weakness: journal entries over £500k lack supporting document requirements and segregation of duties
findings.detail: The audit identifies that journal entries >£500k require approval by a senior colleague but no supporting documents are mandated. Individuals can post and approve their own journals with no segregation of duties. This is flagged as a significant fraud risk requiring AI-driven transaction scoring to identify high-risk entries.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's ability to prevent or detect fraudulent financial statements is materially compromised by control weaknesses in the journal entry process.
findings.figures: £500k threshold; no supporting document requirement
findings.quote: although there is a system control in place whereby individuals need to post a journal with a value of greater than £500k for it to be posted by a more senior colleague, there is no requirement for supporting documents to be added. There is also no imposed segregation of duties, with individuals able to post and approve their own journals.

findings.headline: £140m SEND specialist provision capital committed ahead of government white paper publication
findings.detail: Council has allocated £140m capital for SEND specialist provision and inclusive practices in the budget proposals, with implementation expected to align with a government white paper that has not yet been published. findings.quote: £140m Capital budget in budget proposals to deliver specialist provision, focus on mainstream inclusive practices, expected to be the focus of the White Paper

findings.detail: The capital programme shows £9m of reprogramming from prior years, with delays in tender specification agreement pushing more work into later years. findings.detail: The report states: "The County Council does not hold statutory powers to direct or determine council tax collection practices or the design of Council Tax Support schemes. These functions rest solely with District and Borough Councils as billing authorities." The council can only "engage constructively through established partnership forums, provide data and analysis, and support collaborative work."
findings.matters: This structural constraint means the council cannot unilaterally resolve material revenue challenges; material income pressures (£69.3m CTS impact, collection rate variation) fall outside the council's direct control.

findings.paper_title: 32 Item 12 Motion Report- Council Tax
findings.headline: Hertfordshire's council tax base growth of 0.61% for 2026/27 is less than one-seventh of the six-year average, limiting revenue growth despite stated record housebuilding
findings.detail: Council notes that "growth has been below the national average. This has limited the uplift in Council Tax yield available to support services." The 2026/27 growth rate of 0.61% compares poorly to the prior six years' average of 4.2%. Three Rivers and Watford show particularly weak growth at 0.21% and 0.11% respectively.
findings.matters: Constrained taxbase growth limits the council's ability to grow revenues organically and fund rising service demand; reduces fiscal flexibility at a time of severe financial constraints.

findings.paper_title: 32 Item 12 Motion Report- Council Tax
findings.headline: Hertsmere's council tax base contracted by 210.3 Band D equivalents (0.49%) despite ongoing housebuilding, as rising Council Tax Support claims outpaced dwelling growth
findings.detail: Hertsmere's 2026/27 taxbase fell to 43,121.1 from 43,331.4 Band D equivalents in 2025/26. findings.committee: Local Government Pension Scheme Local Pension Board
findings.paper_title: 02 Item 2 26-27 Pension Fund Treasury Strategy_Final
findings.headline: Employer pension contributions falling while pension payouts rise 3.8%, creating a £3.5m reduction in available annual cash
findings.detail: Following the 2025 actuarial valuation, employer contributions are expected to fall from 1 April 2026, while pension payouts will increase 3.8% based on September 2025 CPI inflation. This tightens the fund's cash position significantly: monthly available cash for other Fund transactions is estimated to fall from approximately £5-7m in 2025/26 to approximately £2m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Falling employer contributions combined with rising payouts signal tightening cash flows in the pension fund and could require the council to increase contributions in future if this trend continues, directly affecting the council's overall financial position.
findings.figures: Employer contributions expected to fall from circa £19-20m to £16.2m monthly; pension payouts increasing 3.8% to £14.2m monthly; available cash declining from £5-7m to £2m monthly; annual reduction of approximately £3.5m.
findings.quote: Following the 2025 Actuarial valuation, it is anticipated that the contributions received from Employers will fall from 1 April 2026 and pensions paid will increase by 3.8%, based on the September 2025 Consumer Price Index rise.

findings.committee: Local Government Pension Scheme Local Pension Board
findings.paper_title: 05 Item 3 Appendix A - Investment Strategy Statement 2026 Draft
findings.headline: Major asset pooling transition may incur unexpected costs
findings.detail: The fund is transitioning all £X billion of assets to Border to Coast Pensions Partnership effective 1 April 2026, alongside 17 other local authority funds. Explicitly flagged: the transition may expose the fund to additional risk and generate unexpected costs, to be managed through professional advice.
findings.matters: Pooling transition costs could be material to the council if the fund bears them directly or if they delay planned investment changes.
findings.figures: 18 funds total joining BCPP; deadline 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The Fund is due to join BCPP and may be exposed to additional risk during the transition of assets to the pool and may incur unexpected costs in relation to the transition of assets among managers. The Fund will seek suitable professional advice during this transition period to budget and manage cost.

findings.committee: Local Government Pension Scheme Local Pension Board
findings.paper_title: 05 Item 3 Appendix A - Investment Strategy Statement 2026 Draft
findings.headline: Cashflow management now central to fund strategy as pension payments exceed contributions
findings.detail: Fund maturity has made cashflow position a key consideration in the investment strategy review. The allocation between liquid and illiquid assets is now deliberately structured around pension payroll and benefit payment flows.
findings.matters: Funds in deficit cashflow require employer injections to meet benefit payments; this directly reduces council liquidity and affects borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Cash holding 1% of portfolio reserved for monthly pension payroll; rest allocated for multi-year benefit obligations
findings.quote: The Fund is gradually becoming more mature and the Cashflow position is monitored by the Fund's Officers and Fund Actuary at each triennial valuation This has become an important consideration in setting and monitoring the Fund's investment strategy and strategic asset allocation to illiquid and liquid assets.

findings.committee: Local Government Pension Scheme Local Pension Board
findings.paper_title: 05 Item 3 Appendix A - Investment Strategy Statement 2026 Draft
findings.headline: Fund maturity driving shift to income generation rather than growth
findings.detail: The fund now needs income over and above employer contributions to pay pensions in cash, rather than relying on asset growth. This has prompted a strategic reallocation toward income-generating assets: bonds (10.5%), index-linked gilts (13.5%), property (12%), infrastructure (6%), and credit instruments (9.5% combined).
findings.matters: A fund that requires supplementary income signals maturing liabilities and rising pension costs. As the fund matures, the council's employer contributions are likely to increase or stabilise at higher levels.
findings.figures: Income-generating assets now 50%+ of portfolio; equity allocation 41.5% (listed 34.5%, private 7%)
findings.quote: The Fund is a long-term investor but requires income over and above contributions received, in order to pay pensions. In light of this, the investment strategy has been developed with a view to generating additional income from alternative assets and bonds, rather than from equities, in order to avoid being a forced seller of assets at a low point in the market.

findings.committee: Local Government Pension Scheme Local Pension Board
findings.paper_title: 04 Item 3 Draft Investment Strategy Statement
findings.headline: Regulatory deadline of 31 March 2026 to approve investment strategy, with further revised version required by September 2026
findings.detail: The current Investment Strategy Statement must be approved by the Pensions Committee by 31 March 2026. Additionally, the Pensions Bill currently in parliament will introduce new regulations (expected to come into force March 2026), requiring a revised ISS within 6 months, by September 2026. Officers will present the revised strategy to the Pension Board in July 2026 following workshops with committee members in advance of that meeting.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance is essential. The compressed timeline to approve the current version and then immediately undertake further revision under new regulations creates governance risk. Failure to meet deadlines would be a compliance breach.
findings.figures: 31 March 2026 approval deadline; September 2026 publication deadline for revised ISS; July 2026 Pension Board meeting for revised strategy.
findings.quote: The ISS must be agreed and approved by the Pensions Committee by the 31 March 2026, as well as presented to the Pension Board before consultation with the employers in the Fund.

findings.committee: Local Government Pension Scheme Local Pension Board
findings.paper_title: 04 Item 3 Draft Investment Strategy Statement
findings.headline: Investment strategy amended to reintroduce hedge funds and reduce bonds following actuarial review
findings.detail: The proposed asset allocation has been changed since December 2025 to shift from a constrained strategy to an unconstrained version. The December proposal had removed Liquid Diversifiers and reweighted into Private Debt and Index Linked Gilts; the revised version reintroduces Hedge Funds and reduces Bonds. Officers and advisors (Mercer) both agree the unconstrained version is more appropriate to deliver the fund's long-term funding target.
findings.matters: Changes to the pension fund's asset allocation affect expected returns and risk profile, which determine whether future employer contributions will need to increase. This signals active management but also reflects uncertainty about the fund's ability to meet its obligations at current contribution levels.

The strategic asset allocation is critical to long-term financial stability: if returns fall short, employer contributions could increase or remain higher for longer. The 2025 Triennial Valuation results (shared confidentially in November 2025) will determine the optimum asset allocation and therefore future contribution rates.
findings.matters: A significant increase in employer contributions would reduce the council's financial flexibility and constrain the budget available for services. This is material to assessing the council's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity.

findings.paper_title: 260217 05A(iii) 2026-27 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Schools High Needs Block deficit reaches £178.5m by March 2027, with government funding solution unconfirmed despite statutory override ending April 2028.
findings.detail: Hertfordshire's High Needs Block is accumulating a massive deficit driven by SEND provision costs. findings.matters: A £178.5m contingent liability on the schools budget represents a major unfunded obligation the council cannot control. This relies on government delivering promised funding that remains unconfirmed, creating significant refinancing risk if arrangements fall short or are delayed beyond April 2028.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Monthly bank reconciliations not being reviewed or documented, creating risk of undetected timing errors
findings.detail: Walkthrough identified a monthly bank reconciliation that had not been reviewed and contained no evidence that a review had occurred. While reviews take place within the team, they are not documented in the accounts system.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation review is fundamental financial controls. An undocumented review creates risk that reconciling items accumulate undetected. Combined with other control deficiencies, this indicates a pattern of weak evidencing of controls.
findings.figures: One unreviewed monthly bank reconciliation identified
findings.quote: During our walkthrough of Cash and Cash Equivalents we identified a monthly bank reconciliation that had not been reviewed and had no evidence of review.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion expected on comparatives due to continuing impacts from disclaimed prior years
findings.detail: A disclaimer of opinion was issued for 2023/24 at the statutory backstop date. For 2024/25, auditors expect to issue a modified audit opinion qualified only in respect of I&E (Income & Expenditure) comparatives as they rebuild assurance. Approximately £930m of land and buildings from 2022/23 revaluations remain unaudited.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion means comparatives cannot be fully relied upon by lenders assessing trend performance. The continued qualification on I&E comparatives affects the ability to assess year-on-year movements in income and expenditure balances.
findings.figures: £930m of unaudited revalued assets from 2022/23
findings.quote: Subject to the satisfactory resolution of our remaining queries on the disclaimed periods, we expect to issue a modified Auditor's Report, qualified only in respect of I&E comparatives.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Pension assumption review lacks objective criteria and documented evidence, despite £627 million net asset position
findings.detail: Management reviews actuarial assumptions used for the £2.985bn pension asset and £2.358bn pension liability, but auditing standards found no established criteria for identifying outliers, no thresholds for escalation, and no documented evidence of review. Management treats this as an annual occurrence but there is insufficient process to meet effective control standards.
findings.matters: The council now holds a £627 million pension net asset position (in surplus for the third consecutive year). Auditing standards require documented management review controls for significant accounting estimates because small changes in discount rates, inflation assumptions, or mortality can swing this estimate by hundreds of millions.
findings.figures: £2,985m gross pension assets; £2,358m gross pension liabilities; net surplus position
findings.quote: We identified that there is no criteria or threshold developed for investigation/identification of outliers for pension assumptions. Therefore, it does not allow for an objective criteria to perform their review on and therefore it is ineffective.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Journal authorization controls allow £500k threshold avoidance; larger transactions lack documented review trail
findings.detail: Only journals exceeding £500k require secondary approval, and where review does occur there is no documented audit trail of what was reviewed. This creates risk that large transactions just below the threshold bypass detection, and that reviews, when they occur, are not evidenced.
findings.matters: A finance director relies on journal controls to prevent unauthorized or erroneous entries. An arbitrary £500k threshold and lack of review documentation mean transactions representing millions could pass without adequate scrutiny, especially given the pattern of other control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £500k threshold; 47 high-risk journal entries tested
findings.quote: We noted that only journals with individual lines above £500k require secondary approval, and where such journals are reviewed there is an inadequate audit trail to show that the review has taken place.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Property register errors required £7.975 million correction to land and buildings valuations
findings.detail: A rural property was duplicated in the fixed asset register (Holme Farm, £8.830m overstatement) and another property that had been split was partially omitted (Dunsley Farm Brewery, £855k understatement), requiring a net correction of £7.975m to the £2.824 billion land and buildings balance.
findings.matters: Asset register errors indicate control weaknesses over the council's largest asset class. A £7.975m correction represents material adjustment to property records and raises questions about the accuracy of the rolling revaluation programme over £2.8bn of assets.
findings.figures: £2,824m total land and buildings NBV at 31 March 2024; £8.830k duplicate asset; £855k missing asset; £7.975k net adjustment
findings.quote: We identified one rural asset where the categorisation of the asset had changed but this had resulted in a duplicate asset in the fixed asset register. The duplicate asset valuation of £8,830k was therefore overstated... one rural asset that had been split where one of the subsequent components was not included in the FAR. The component's value of £855k was therefore understated.

findings.paper_title: 02a. Appendix A HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Prior year pension deficit overstated by £53 million due to actuarial error that went undetected
findings.detail: The previous actuary applied a contribution rate of 0.9% instead of 0.1% when calculating the asset ceiling under IFRIC 14 for the pension scheme, overstating the council's pension liability by £53 million. This error was not caught by controls and only emerged when the new actuary reviewed the work.
findings.matters: A £53 million error in one of the largest balance sheet items shows prior controls around complex pension accounting were ineffective, and undermines confidence in the reliability of prior period figures even after restatement.
findings.figures: £53 million overstatement
findings.quote: We have also identified a difference in prior period relating to the calculation of the asset ceiling under IFRIC 14. The prior year actuary applied a secondary contribution rate of 0.9% instead of the correct rate of 0.1%, as confirmed by the Council and used by Barnet Waddingham (the new actuary) in the current year. This resulted in an overstatement of the additional liability and the net pensions deficit by approximately £53 million.

findings.paper_title: 07. SEND Improvement Update
findings.headline: Additional £6.3m revenue investment approved for SEND services in 2026/27 to meet growing need
findings.detail: The draft Council Budget proposes an additional £6.3m revenue investment in SEND services for 2026/27 to support growing need and further improvements. This is on top of £7m approved in 2024/25 and £2.8m rising to £4.6m in 2025/26. The ongoing requirement for annual increases suggests structural demand outpacing available funding.
findings.matters: Year-on-year need for additional revenue investment to maintain service levels indicates demand is outpacing available resources and suggests future budget pressure if growth continues.
findings.figures: £6.3m increase in revenue for SEND services in 2026/27; number of EHCPs up 18% to Nov 2025 compared to previous year
findings.quote: Through the Council's draft budget for 2026/27 – 2029/30, it is proposed an additional £6.3m revenue will be invested in SEND Services to support growing need, with the number of EHCPs up 18% to Nov 2025 compared to previous year

findings.paper_title: 07. SEND Improvement Update
findings.headline: £140m capital programme for SEND provision proposed, requiring significant council investment despite existing funding constraints
findings.detail: The draft Council Budget 2026/27-2029/30 proposes a £140m capital programme for specialist provision places, part-funded by a recent £3bn central government grant. However, the programme is being proposed despite the council facing a stated significant deficit, indicating capital spending is not discretionary but driven by statutory demand.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments on top of existing revenue deficits require careful management and signal the council is operating under significant pressure to meet statutory obligations with constrained resources.
findings.figures: £140m capital programme proposed for 2026/27-2029/30; part-funded by central government's £3 billion grant announcement
findings.quote: a £140m capital programme is proposed to support development of further specialist provision places and deliver the SEND Provision Plan, in response to growing needs.

findings.paper_title: 07. SEND Improvement Update
findings.headline: Hertfordshire is an outlier nationally for high permanent exclusion rates among EHCP pupils
findings.detail: Permanent exclusion rates have increased in the 2025/26 academic year, with exclusion rates for EHCP pupils particularly high. The document explicitly states Hertfordshire is an outlier compared to both national figures and statistical neighbours. Active work is underway to address this, but it signals a significant governance and service delivery issue.
findings.matters: Being an outlier for exclusion rates among vulnerable pupils indicates systemic issues in inclusion provision, potential reputational risk, and possible future liability or regulatory attention from DfE.
findings.figures: Permanent exclusion rates higher in 2025/26 than first half term of 2024/25; Hertfordshire identified as outlier nationally and compared to statistical neighbours
findings.quote: Permanent Exclusion notifications are higher than the first half term of 2024/25 and permanently exclusions for EHCPs are particularly high. Hertfordshire is an outlier in terms of a high exclusion rate for EHCP Pupils nationally and compared to statistical neighbours.

findings.paper_title: 07. SEND Improvement Update
findings.headline: EHCP demand growing 18% year-on-year, exceeding available provision and planned capacity
findings.detail: The EHCP cohort increased 18% to November 2025 compared to the previous year (15,125 total). Children agreed for specialist provision continue to exceed availability locally. The document notes resources are stretched to deliver for more children with the same resources, directly impacting service capacity.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing demand for a statutory service that the council must fund, combined with inability to meet all needs locally, indicates structural overspend risk and potential reliance on out-of-county placements (more expensive).
findings.figures: 15,125 EHCPs at end Nov 2025, up 18% on same period previous year; 704 children placed in specialist provision in 2025/26 by Nov, compared to 942 for whole of 2024/25
findings.quote: the number of EHCPs has increased to 15,125 at end of Nov 2025, up 18% on same period previous year... the number of children being agreed for provision continues to exceed the availability of provision locally

findings.paper_title: 07. SEND Improvement Update
findings.headline: Significant deficit in high needs funding with no solution beyond campaigning for national formula change
findings.detail: Hertfordshire is the ninth lowest funded area for high needs funding and faces a significant deficit both this year and in years to come. The council is part of the f40 group campaigning for revisions to the High Needs Funding formula to make it more equitable, but this is a long-term lobbying effort, not a funded solution. The deficit directly impacts provision available for children and young people.
findings.matters: A structural funding deficit in a statutory service that the council must provide signals persistent budget pressure and limited flexibility to meet growing demand without either drawing reserves or reducing service quality.
findings.figures: Ninth lowest funded area for high needs funding; significant deficit in this financial year and years to come
findings.quote: Hertfordshire is the ninth lowest funded area for high needs funding, and the Council is facing a significant deficit in this financial year and years to come.

findings.paper_title: 03a Item 3 Appendix A - Draft HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Fixed asset register contained duplicate and missing property valuations requiring downward adjustments of £7,975k.
findings.detail: Audit testing identified one rural property (Holme Farm) that had been duplicated in the fixed asset register with an overstatement of £8,830k. Additionally, another rural property (Dunsley Farm Brewery) had been split from the farm in a prior year but only the farm was recorded, understating that component by £855k. The net correction reduced the fixed asset net book value by £7,975k. Management investigated to ensure no further duplicates existed.
findings.matters: Material errors in the property register indicate potential weakness in asset tracking and valuation controls, and suggest the balance sheet may contain other undetected misstatements.
findings.figures: £8,830k duplicate overstatement (Holme Farm); £855k understatement (Dunsley Farm Brewery); net adjustment of £7,975k downward
findings.quote: We identified one rural asset where the categorisation of the asset had changed but this had resulted in a duplicate asset in the fixed asset register. The duplicate asset valuation of £8,830k was therefore overstated. The component's value of £855k was therefore understated. Management have therefore adjusted Note 12 to reflect the overall decrease in Net Book Value by £7975k.

findings.paper_title: 03a Item 3 Appendix A - Draft HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Approximately £930 million of property assets from 2022/23 remain unaudited and are still undergoing assurance-building procedures.
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimed audit opinion for 2022/23 (from previous auditors) and 2023/24 (KPMG), following the government's audit backlog measures. The council is working to rebuild assurance on these prior-year balances. Unaudited assets from 2022/23 valued at around £930m create uncertainty about the opening balance sheet position for 2024/25, particularly as any assets with significant changes require revaluation.
findings.matters: Unaudited opening balances represent a material uncertainty over the integrity of the balance sheet, affecting the council's financial position and the reliability of comparatives.
findings.figures: £930 million of unaudited 2022/23 property assets; disclaimed opinions for years ending 31 March 2023 and 2024
findings.quote: The value of these unaudited assets is c.£930m however any asset within this balance with a significant change in condition or use would also be subject to revaluation in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 03a Item 3 Appendix A - Draft HCC ISA260 24-25
findings.headline: Prior-year pension deficit was overstated by approximately £53 million due to an actuary calculation error in 2023/24.
findings.detail: The previous year's actuary used an incorrect secondary contribution rate of 0.9% instead of 0.1% when calculating the asset ceiling under IFRIC 14, resulting in a material overstatement of the pension deficit. This significantly changes the council's financial position from what was previously reported. The council is now in surplus for the third consecutive year.
findings.matters: A £53m correction to pension liabilities materially affects the council's balance sheet and financial standing, which is critical information for assessing borrowing capacity and financial health.
findings.figures: £53 million overstatement of pension deficit in prior year; Council now in pension surplus for third consecutive year
findings.quote: The prior year actuary applied a secondary contribution rate of 0.9% instead of the correct rate of 0.1%, as confirmed by the Council and used by Barnet Waddingham in the current year. This resulted in an overstatement of the additional liability and the net pensions deficit by approximately £53 million.

findings.paper_title: 06 Item 6 Treasury management mid year report 2025-26 final
findings.headline: High Needs education deficit growing to £88m as grant funding fails to meet demand for SEND provision
findings.detail: The High Needs block, which funds education for children with special educational needs, had a £26m deficit at end of 2024/25 and is forecast to increase by a further £62m during 2025/26. This represents a structural mismatch where the dedicated schools grant is insufficient to meet actual demand for SEND education, forcing the council to fund the shortfall through borrowing and incurring additional interest costs.
findings.matters: Lenders must understand structural drains on council cash flow where statutory obligations exceed central government funding. This council's large and growing High Needs shortfall signals ongoing pressure on finances and borrowing requirements that cannot be managed through efficiency savings or one-off actions.
findings.figures: £26m deficit at end 2024/25, forecast increase of £62m during 2025/26
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25, the deficit on the High Needs block was £26m. This is forecast to increase by a further £62m during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 07a. Item 7 Appendix A - Corporate Risks not at Target for December 2025 AC Final
findings.headline: Major HCC development schemes stalling — Gilston judicial review ongoing, negative appeal prompts review of exit terms
findings.detail: HCC holds land in major developments (Gilston, Hemel, Brookfield, Baldock) expected to generate financial returns. Gilston is subject to ongoing judicial review; Hemel applications expected late 2025. A recent negative planning appeal has prompted review of HCC's legal 'walkaway clause', indicating consideration of early exits from schemes.
findings.matters: Development returns are core to long-term asset strategy and revenue forecasts. Judicial reviews, negative appeals, and contemplated exits reduce confidence in expected income and increase carrying costs.
findings.figures: £41.7m in S106/CIL funding secured in 2024/2025; Gilston subject to ongoing judicial review; Baldock outline application submitted Oct 2025; Hemel plan applications expected late 2025
findings.quote: Risks to HCC financial returns from major developments on it's land holdings

findings.paper_title: 07a. Item 7 Appendix A - Corporate Risks not at Target for December 2025 AC Final
findings.headline: SEND costs rising faster than capacity — £80.2m special school budget in 25/26 yet risk remains 'High, Likely'
findings.detail: Despite £47.3m investment in mainstream funding since 2023 and £104m capital investment in 25/26, SEND risk is rated 'High impact, Likely' with no improvement from current to target level. Alternative provision costs have doubled since 2023 (33 framework plus 87 spot contract providers). Numbers of children with EHCPs continue to rise, and the council is placing 942 children per year.
findings.matters: SEND is statutory and demand-led — the council cannot refuse it. Heavy spending has not reduced risk, suggesting underlying demand outpaces supply and long-term cost containment is uncertain.
findings.figures: Maintained special school budget £63.7m (23/24) rising to £80.2m (25/26); £47.3m investment in mainstream funding since 2023; alternative provision costs up 100% since 2023; 942 placements in 24/25; £104m capital investment in 25/26
findings.quote: Failure to maintain sustainability and pace of SEND improvements and meeting statutory SEND duties

findings.paper_title: 06 Item 4 Motion Report Highways Locality Budget
findings.headline: Highways Locality Budget frozen at £90,000 per councillor for 15 years despite cumulative inflation erosion.
findings.detail: The budget has remained unchanged since 2010/11. If indexed to inflation, it would be approximately £135,000 per councillor today, representing a real-terms shortfall of around £45,000 per councillor. This implies total highways service delivery capacity has declined significantly in real terms over this period.
findings.matters: Shows a core service suffering chronic underfunding, indicating the council accepts declining service capacity rather than adjusting allocations for inflation—a sign of budget rigidity.
findings.figures: £90,000 current, £135,000 inflation-indexed, £45,000 per councillor shortfall, £3.51m additional annual cost if fully indexed
findings.quote: That the Highways Locality Budget has remained fixed at £90,000 per County Councillor since its introduction in the 2010/11 financial year
